result.summary: Minerva inspires Diomed, who slaughters Trojans, is wounded by Pandarus, then kills Pandarus, fells Aeneas with a stone and wounds Venus when she rescues him. With Minerva's help he then wounds Mars, who flees to Olympus and is healed, while the gods quarrel and the battle swings back and forth.

scenes.title: Diomed's aristeia begins
scenes.summary: Minerva inspires Diomed, who kills Phegeus. Minerva draws Mars aside and the Achaean chieftains kill many Trojans while Diomed rages like a torrent.
scenes.stakes: Trojans face rout; Diomed seeks glory and Idaeus barely escapes death.

scenes.title: Pandarus wounds Diomed
scenes.summary: Pandarus shoots Diomed, who has Sthenelus pull out the arrow and prays to Minerva. She renews him, warns him to fight only Venus among the gods, and he kills many Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Diomed is wounded and might die; Trojans are being slaughtered.

scenes.title: Pandarus dies, Aeneas falls
scenes.summary: Aeneas and Pandarus attack Diomed in a chariot. Diomed kills Pandarus and crushes Aeneas' hip with a stone, but Venus lifts Aeneas away.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas and Pandarus risk death against Diomed; Aeneas would have died without Venus.

scenes.title: Diomed wounds Venus
scenes.summary: Sthenelus secures Aeneas' horses. Diomed pursues Venus, wounds her hand, and Apollo takes Aeneas away.
scenes.stakes: Venus is hurt and Aeneas is in danger of being killed.

scenes.title: Venus on Olympus
scenes.summary: Venus borrows Mars' chariot and goes to Olympus, where Dione comforts her with tales of gods hurt by mortals. Minerva and Juno mock her and Jove tells her to leave war.
scenes.stakes: Venus is in pain and humiliated.

scenes.title: Apollo, Mars and the Trojan rally
scenes.summary: Diomed attacks Aeneas, but Apollo drives him back and has Aeneas healed in Pergamus. Mars rallies the Trojans, Sarpedon rebukes Hector, and Aeneas returns.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas' life; Trojan morale and Hector's honour.

scenes.title: Battle surges back and forth
scenes.summary: Agamemnon, Aeneas, Menelaus, Antilochus, Hector and Ajax trade blows. Diomed warns his men against fighting the god beside Hector.
scenes.stakes: Warriors on both sides risk death; the Achaeans may be forced back by Mars.

scenes.title: Sarpedon and Tlepolemus
scenes.summary: Tlepolemus and Sarpedon fight; Tlepolemus dies and Sarpedon is wounded. Ulysses kills many Lycians and Hector and Mars press the Argives.
scenes.stakes: Sarpedon might die; the Argives are pressed by Mars and Hector.

scenes.title: Juno and Minerva arm
scenes.summary: Juno and Minerva arm, ride from Olympus after Jove allows Juno to oppose Mars, and arrive at Troy.
scenes.stakes: Argive losses to Mars threaten the gods' promise to Menelaus.

scenes.title: Diomed wounds Mars
scenes.summary: Juno rouses the Argives. Minerva joins Diomed in his chariot and drives his spear into Mars, who roars and ascends to heaven.
scenes.stakes: Diomed risks fighting a god; Mars could kill him.

scenes.title: Mars healed on Olympus
scenes.summary: Mars complains to Jove, who rebukes him but has Paeeon heal him. Juno and Minerva return to Olympus.
scenes.stakes: Mars is in pain and risks Jove's anger.

characters.name: Tlepolemus

characters.name: Hercules

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Minerva, the Roman name for Athena.
Title of Venus, linked to Cyprus.

notable_quotes.reason: Diomed taunts Venus, telling her war is not for a goddess of love.
Jove tells Venus she is not meant for war but marriage.
Agamemnon's maxim that those who shun dishonour more often live.

analysis.text: Diomed's aristeia shows a mortal at the peak of heroic prowess, even challenging gods with divine backing, while the gods' squabbles mirror human conflict.
The catalogue of killings and genealogies reflects oral epic tradition, honouring warriors and their families and the heroic code of glory.

legacy.text: The wounding of gods by a mortal in Book 5 was much discussed by ancient critics and later poets; Aeneas' rescue by Venus prefigures his role in Virgil's Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: The text explains that gods bleed ichor rather than blood because they do not eat bread or drink wine.

language_notes.text: The star is Sirius, whose bright rising in late summer was thought to bring fever; its 'bath' in Oceanus means rising from the sea-encircling river at the world's edge.
'Bestride' means to stand over a fallen body to defend it from stripping of armour.
'Vouchsafe' means to grant graciously; Minerva speaks as if the victory were Jove's gift to give.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans and Argives.
Alexandrus is Paris. His ships carried Helen off from Greece, the act that began the war.
'Bastard' here means a son born outside marriage; Theano raising him anyway shows her loyalty to her husband Antenor.
Cuirass: a piece of body armour covering the chest and back, here made of metal.
"Knights Trojans" means Trojan horsemen or warriors; "knights" is the translator's word for chariot-fighting nobles.
Vaunt means to boast.
"Aegis-bearing Jove": Jove (the Greek Zeus) carries the aegis, a fearsome goatskin shield or cape; here it describes him as Minerva's father.
"Unweariable" means tireless, an address to Minerva (the Greek Athena).
Minerva gives Diomed the power to see which figures on the battlefield are gods, normally hidden from mortals.
"Reader of dreams" means an interpreter of dreams, a seer who explained their meaning.
Begat means fathered.
"In respect of which" means "in which": no man at Troy, and none in Lycia, is Pandarus's equal as an archer.
"Cuirass" is a breastplate; the "breast-piece" is the same armour, so the two words name one defence.
The horses of Tros descend from the stock Jove gave Tros, an early king of Troy, as compensation for his son Ganymede.
"Vouchsafes" means graciously grants.
"Spring Aeneas' horses" means to leap on them and seize them, then drive them to the Achaean lines.
"Stole the blood" means secretly bred his mares with the divine stallions to get their offspring, without Laomedon's permission.
"As men now are" refers to the belief that heroes of the past were far stronger than later humans.
Venus conceived Aeneas with the mortal Anchises while he herded cattle on Mount Ida; this is why Aeneas is her son.
"Hurly-burly" means the noise and confusion of battle; Sthenelus ties his own team out of the fighting.
"The Cyprian goddess" is Venus, associated with Cyprus, a main centre of her worship.
Ichor is the thin fluid that serves as blood in the gods; the narrator explains it by their diet of ambrosia and nectar.
"Danaan" is another name for the Greeks, as is Achaean.
"Besmirched" means soiled or stained.
"Gold-bedizened" means gaudily decked out in gold.
"Nothing loth" means willingly; "in a trice" means in an instant.
Otus and Ephialtes were giant brothers who tried to assault the gods and once captured Mars.
The son of Amphitryon is Hercules, who wounded gods in his own exploits.
"Recked not" means took no heed of; Dione is speaking of Hercules.
Minerva sarcastically hints that Venus was scratched while seducing a Greek woman to follow a Trojan, mocking her role as goddess of love.
"With might and main" means with all one's strength; "thrice... and the fourth time" is a traditional Homeric pattern before a divine rebuke.
A "wraith" here is a phantom double, an image shaped to look like Aeneas so the fighting continues around it.
The "Cyprian" is Venus (Aphrodite), whose hand Diomed wounded earlier in this book when she tried to rescue Aeneas.
Sarpedon recalls Hector's boast that he needed no allies, since his own kin could defend Troy.
Winnowing is tossing grain in the wind so the light chaff blows away from the heavy kernels.
Pallas Minerva (the Greek Athena) has been aiding the Danaans (Greeks); Mars acts once she withdraws.
Danaans is one of Homer's names for the Greeks, along with Achaeans and Argives, all used interchangeably in this translation.
Boreas is the North Wind personified; the son of Saturn is Jove (the Greek Zeus), who gathers clouds.
Descent from a river god Alpheus is a heroic genealogy; rivers were worshipped as divine ancestors. Pylians are the people of Nestor's Pylos.
Ilius is another name for Troy (Ilium), the city the Greeks besiege.
Mars egged him on so that Menelaus would be killed: the war god favours the Trojans and pushes Menelaus toward a fatal duel.
He stood head-down in the sand: the dying Mydon is stuck upside down, a grim image, until the horses knock him flat.
Enyo is a goddess of war and battle-din who accompanies Mars (the Greek Ares).
His lot had led him: fate, not choice, brought Amphius to fight for Priam, adding pathos to his death.
Hercules sacked Troy earlier because king Laomedon cheated him of the promised horses. Ilius is another name for Troy.
"Hades of the noble steeds" is a fixed epithet for the god of the dead; "yield glory to myself" means Sarpedon will win the glory.
Ulysses is the Greek hero; the son of Jove here is Sarpedon, whom fate does not allow Ulysses to kill.
Jove's oak tree was a sacred landmark near Troy's walls, mentioned elsewhere in the poem.
Argives and Danaans, like Achaeans, are names for the Greeks; Mars is the war god (Greek Ares).
Argives: one of Homer's names for the Greeks, from Argos. Achaeans and Danaans are also used.
Gainsay means to contradict or oppose; Minerva simply agreed.
Gold-bedizened means gaudily or richly decked out with gold.
Felloes are the outer rims of a wheel; the tire is the metal band around them.
Naves are the hubs of the wheels, the central parts through which the axle runs.
Rout means panicked flight in battle. The aegis is Jove's divine shield or goatskin cape, here fringed with terrifying figures.
Nothing loth means not unwilling, that is, eagerly.
Ambrosia is the food of the gods; here it serves as fodder for the immortal horses.
The sentence is grammatically broken: 'if his spear was so deadly' reflects the translator's rendering of a reproach contrasting Achilles' fighting days with the present.
Refers to Tydeus's embassy to Thebes, where he challenged the Cadmeans (Thebans) to contests and won them all, before they ambushed him on his way home.
Aegis-bearing: Jove carries the aegis, a fearsome goatskin shield or cape, a standard epithet of his.
'Villain incarnate' means evil in bodily form; Minerva accuses Mars of switching sides, as the next lines explain.
The helmet of Hades made its wearer invisible; Minerva uses it so Mars cannot see her.
A termagant is a violent, quarrelsome, scolding woman; Mars means Minerva, Jove's daughter, who helped Diomed against him.
The Cyprian is Venus, associated with Cyprus. Diomed wounded her earlier in this book while she rescued her son Aeneas.
"Sir Facing-both-ways" is a sarcastic nickname: Jove calls Mars two-faced or changeable, perhaps for helping first one side and then the other.
The Titans were the older gods defeated by Jove and imprisoned in Tartarus, so lying lower than them means the deepest punishment.
Paeeon is the physician of the gods. "Not of mortal mould" means Mars is immortal, so he can be healed quickly.
"Of Argos" and "of Alalcomene" are epithets naming the places where Juno and Minerva were worshipped.

context_notes.text: Pallas Minerva (the Greek Athena) is goddess of war and wisdom, and she favours the Achaeans and Diomed.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the smith god of fire, which explains why he rescues his priest's son.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war and favours the Trojans here, so Minerva must remove him.
The Scamander is the river of Troy's plain, also worshipped as a god.
Diana (the Greek Artemis) is goddess of the hunt and wild animals.
Pandarus, son of Lycaon, came from Lycia and was an archer favoured by Apollo, the god of archery.
Tydeus, Diomed's father, was a famed warrior who fought in the earlier expedition against Thebes, where Minerva had helped him.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) is the goddess of love and a supporter of Troy, and she is not a warrior goddess, so she can be wounded.
Priam is the aged king of Troy; Echemmon and Chromius are two of his sons.
Pandarus is a Lycian ally of Troy, famed as an archer. He has just wounded Diomed with an arrow.
Sthenelus is Diomed's friend and charioteer. Aeneas is a Trojan prince, son of the goddess Venus (the Greek Aphrodite).
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is the goddess of war and wisdom. She is favouring Diomed throughout this book.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war. Glutting him with blood means killing a warrior.
Minerva and Enyo are war goddesses; Venus is a goddess of love and has no real power in battle.
Dione is named here as Venus' mother; in this version Venus is the daughter of Jove and Dione.
Aegialeia is Diomed's wife; the prediction hints at his death, though in the Iliad he survives.
Pergamus was Troy's citadel, with a temple of Apollo, who favours the Trojans.
Latona is Apollo's mother and Diana his sister; both side with Troy and heal Aeneas.
Sarpedon, son of Jove, leads the Lycians, Trojan allies from Asia Minor, far from home.
The son of Atreus is Agamemnon, king of Mycenae and commander of the Greek army.
The Paphlagonians were a people of northern Asia Minor who fought as Trojan allies.
Gods intervene directly in Homeric battles; Diomed can see the god because Minerva earlier cleared his sight in this book.
Tlepolemus, son of Hercules, led Greek troops from Rhodes. Sarpedon, a son of Jove, led the Lycians, Trojan allies.
Jove protects his son Sarpedon, though he will let him die later in the poem.
Heroes in the Iliad are often revived by divine or natural means; the north wind here restores Sarpedon.
Juno (the Greek Hera) favours the Greeks. Mars (Ares), god of war, is helping the Trojans here.
Hebe is the goddess of youth and a daughter of Jove and Juno; she serves the gods.
The Gorgon's head, Medusa's, was said to turn onlookers to stone. It appears on the aegis as a terrifying emblem.
The Cyprian is Venus (Aphrodite), associated with Cyprus. She and Apollo support the Trojans.
Diomed (Diomedes) is the Greek hero whose great deeds fill this book. Stentor was a herald famed for his huge voice.
Pandarus, a Trojan archer, had earlier wounded Diomed with an arrow; Minerva now finds him tending the injury.
Minerva had earlier granted Diomed power to recognise gods and told him to fight only Venus among the gods.
Sthenelus is Diomed's friend and charioteer, so Minerva takes his place beside Diomed.
Mars is the god of war, fighting here for the Trojans, though he had promised Juno and Minerva to help the Argives.
Gods in Homer bleed a bloodlike fluid called ichor, which is why the wound shows "immortal blood."
Hebe, goddess of youth, is a cupbearer and attendant of the gods, here serving as a nurse.

literary_notes.text: Diomed's blazing armour is compared to the brilliant summer star, marking him as divinely empowered and dazzling to enemies.
Nearly identical wording for Odius's and Scamandrius's deaths (sentence 19) shows the formulaic, relentless style of Homeric battle scenes.
The hunter taught by Diana is killed in the back while fleeing; his skill and the goddess cannot save him.
Calling the ships the beginning of mischief points to the doom that will fall on Troy and Paris.
The flooding torrent that breaks dykes and walls conveys Diomed's unstoppable force and the helpless Trojan ranks.
Diomed, wounded yet more furious, is compared to a lion wounded by a shepherd, which is still dangerous to the helpless sheep.
The dream-reader's sons are killed, and the seer could not foresee or prevent their deaths, which is grimly ironic.
The aged father's grief and the division of his wealth by kinsmen show the human cost of Diomed's triumph.
A second lion comparison, now of a predator on helpless cattle, stresses how easily Diomed overpowers the two princes.
Pandarus's long self-reproach about his horses and his unused chariots shows him as regretful, domestic and somewhat unheroic.
Diomed says Pandarus has missed, and a moment later Pandarus is killed by the spear that Minerva guides.
Aeneas is compared to a lion standing over the body. The image conveys his fierce, protective strength.
The stone that two men could not lift shows how superhuman Diomed's strength is, aided by Minerva.
"The darkness of night" figures the loss of consciousness as night falling over the eyes.
Diomed taunts Venus for meddling, mocking her as a goddess of seduction only, which belittles her divine status.
Venus exaggerates one wound into a claim that the whole war has changed its nature.
Dione's warning that no man who fights gods lives long to see his children hints at fates awaiting Diomed.
Minerva's mock politeness makes a barbed joke at Venus' expense, casting her wound as a love-affair accident.
Jove's gentle dismissal defines Venus' proper sphere as love and marriage, not war.
Diomed charging "as though he were a god" shows his reckless overreach, which Apollo's warning about mortals and immortals then corrects.
Comparing Hector's kin to hounds cowering before a lion mocks their cowardice and makes the Trojan defenders seem weak.
Men caught in a net conveys helpless capture, warning Hector of Troy's possible fate.
The winnowing scene turns battle dust into drifting chaff, whitening the Achaeans and giving the fight a homely, rural image.
The Greek line standing firm is compared to windless clouds on mountains, conveying calm, immovable resolve amid chaos.
The brothers are likened to lions that raid homesteads until killed, then to fallen pines, showing both their prowess and their downfall.
Calling the dead brothers 'poor fellows' invites sympathy for the fallen.
Diomed's retreat is compared to a traveller halted by a swollen river, showing even a great hero must yield to overwhelming force.
Tlepolemus's taunt shows his arrogance and haste; insulting Sarpedon's parentage is typical heroic pre-battle boasting.
"Darkness of death fell upon his eyes" is a formulaic image presenting death as darkness.
The narrator asks who died first and last, a convention that introduces a catalogue of the slain.
Descriptions like "renowned charioteer" and "of the gleaming girdle" briefly give each victim identity before his death.
Rout, Strife, Strength and Panic are given bodies on the aegis, making abstract terrors of war into visible emblems.
The horses' single leap is measured by the farthest sight across the sea, conveying their divine, superhuman speed.
Likening the goddesses to turtledoves in flight stresses their eagerness and lightness, though they are going to war.
Comparing the fighters to lions and boars, and Juno's shout to Stentor's, conveys their ferocity and the volume of her cry.
Tydeus is portrayed as small but fierce and headstrong, a model Minerva uses to goad Diomed.
The groaning axle conveys the divine weight of the goddess through sound.
Mars's roar equals ten thousand men, showing his divine power and the wound's severity.
Mars's ascent is compared to a dark storm cloud rising after heat, giving the wounded god's departure a menacing grandeur.
Mars's complaint shows him as self-pitying and petulant, blaming others for pain he suffered in the war he loves.
Jove's harsh rejection contrasts with his reluctant care; he hates Mars yet cannot leave his own child in pain.
The epic simile compares Paeeon's swift cure to fig juice curdling milk, giving a homely image of sudden change.
